title: Gender Disparities in Hiring & Political Influence
text:
This project examines gender based disparities in hiring patterns across industries and explores how political influence measured by state political lean (red vs. blue) shapes employment outcomes for men and women in 2024.
Using the Lightcast dataset as our baseline, we apply a structured ETL pipeline to extract, clean, and analyze real world job market data, publishing our findings as an evolving research portfolio.

title: Live Demo: K-Means Clustering
text:
This is an interactive view of the K-Means model from the Predictive Modeling page, kept on its own so you can play with it without scrolling through the full analysis. Each point is a worker placed by age and annual wage, the two features the model used, and colored by the segment K-Means assigned. The black diamonds are the cluster centroids, the center points the algorithm computed for each segment.
Two ways to interact. Use the dropdown to isolate a single segment, or choose “All segments” to see them together. You can also click any entry in the legend to hide or show that segment, and you can box-zoom into any region of the chart. The points shown here are a representative sample so the page stays responsive; the full version that plots all 1.49 million workers runs in the notebook analysis/ml_kmeans_julie.ipynb.


Code
import sys, pathlib
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.io as pio
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"

root = pathlib.Path.cwd()
while not (root / "_quarto.yml").exists() and root != root.parent:
    root = root.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(root / "analysis"))
from utils import apply_theme, PROCESSED

profile = pd.read_csv(PROCESSED / "kmeans_cluster_profile.csv")
profile = profile.sort_values("wgt_avg_wage").reset_index(drop=True)
SEGMENTS = ["Low-wage, early career", "Mid-wage, late career",
            "High-wage professional", "Elite earners"]
profile["segment"] = SEGMENTS[: len(profile)]
cluster_to_segment = dict(zip(profile["cluster"], profile["segment"]))

samp = pd.read_csv(PROCESSED / "kmeans_scatter_sample.csv")
samp["segment"] = samp["cluster"].map(cluster_to_segment)
COLORS = dict(zip(SEGMENTS, ["#2c7bb6", "#fdae61", "#1a9641", "#d7191c"]))

fig = go.Figure()
for seg in SEGMENTS:
    s = samp[samp["segment"] == seg]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scattergl(
        x=s["AGE"], y=s["INCWAGE"], mode="markers", name=seg,
        marker=dict(size=5, opacity=0.5, color=COLORS[seg]),
    ))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=profile["wgt_avg_age"], y=profile["wgt_avg_wage"], mode="markers",
    name="Centroid", hovertext=profile["segment"], hoverinfo="text",
    marker=dict(symbol="diamond", size=15, color="black"),
))

n = len(SEGMENTS)
def visibility(active):
    seg_vis = [True] * n if active is None else [i == active for i in range(n)]
    return seg_vis + [True]            # centroid trace always on

buttons = [dict(label="All segments", method="update",
                args=[{"visible": visibility(None)}])]
for i, seg in enumerate(SEGMENTS):
    buttons.append(dict(label=seg, method="update",
                        args=[{"visible": visibility(i)}]))

fig.update_layout(
    updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, x=0.0, xanchor="left",
                      y=1.15, yanchor="top", showactive=True)],
    xaxis_title="Age", yaxis_title="Annual wage (USD)",
    title="K-Means worker segments (interactive)",
)
apply_theme(fig)
fig.show()

title: Live Demo: K-Means Clustering
text:
What to look for
Switching between segments makes the model’s logic concrete. The low-wage and mid-wage segments sit as broad bands near the bottom and are close to gender balanced, the high-wage professional band sits clearly above them, and the elite segment is a thin scatter far up the wage axis. Isolating the elite segment shows how few workers reach it and, on the full analysis page, how strongly male it skews. The centroids mark where each segment centers, which is exactly the average age and wage of its members.

    'MSA_NAME_INCOMING',

    'NAICS2',
    'NAICS2_NAME',
    'NAICS4',

    'SOC_5',
    'SOC_5_NAME',
    'ONET',

import pandas as pd
import os
def load(df: pd.DataFrame, output_path: str) -> None:
    """
    Save a cleaned DataFrame to CSV in data/processed/.
    Creates the output directory if it doesn't exist.
    Prints confirmation with row/col count and file size.

    Args:
        df          : cleaned DataFrame from transform step
        output_path : destination path e.g. 'data/processed/lightcast_clean.csv'
    """
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(output_path), exist_ok=True)

    print(f"[load] Saved  : {output_path}")

import pandas as pd

def extract(filepath, sample=None):
    if sample:
        df = pd.read_csv(filepath, nrows=sample, low_memory=False)
    else:
        chunks = []
        for chunk in pd.read_csv(filepath, chunksize=500_000, low_memory=False):
            chunks.append(chunk)
        df = pd.concat(chunks, ignore_index=True)

    pd.set_option('display.max_columns', None)
    print("Shape:", df.shape)
    print("\nColumns:", df.columns.tolist())
    print("\nDtypes:\n", df.dtypes)
    print("\nHead:")
    display(df.head(5))
    print("\nTail:")
    display(df.tail(5))
    print("\nMissing values:\n", df.isnull().sum())
    print("\nBasic stats:")
    display(df.describe())

    return df

AD688 Group B — Gender Disparities in Hiring & Political Influence
Defines the load() function used by etl_pipeline.ipynb. Can also be run standalone to re-save an already-transformed DataFrame.
Usage from etl_pipeline.ipynb:
import pandas as pd
import os
def load(df: pd.DataFrame, output_path: str) -> None:
    """
    Save a cleaned DataFrame to CSV in data/processed/.
    Creates the output directory if it doesn't exist.
    Prints confirmation with row/col count and file size.

    Args:
        df          : cleaned DataFrame from transform step
        output_path : destination path e.g. 'data/processed/lightcast_clean.csv'
    """
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(output_path), exist_ok=True)
    df.to_csv(output_path, index=False)

    size_kb = os.path.getsize(output_path) / 1024
    print(f"[load] Saved  : {output_path}")
    print(f"[load] Shape  : {df.shape}")
    print(f"[load] Size   : {size_kb:.1f} KB")

import pandas as pd

def transform(df):
    # Select columns relevant to gender & political analysis
    keep_cols = [
    # Identity / posting metadata
    'ID',
    'LAST_UPDATED_DATE',
    'POSTED',

    # Job content
    'TITLE_CLEAN',          # replaces TITLE_NAME (which is dropped)

    'BODY',

    'COMPANY_NAME',
    'COMPANY_IS_STAFFING',

    # Education
    'EDUCATION_LEVELS',
    'EDUCATION_LEVELS_NAME',

    'MAX_EDULEVELS_NAME',

    # Employment conditions
    'EMPLOYMENT_TYPE_NAME',
    'REMOTE_TYPE_NAME',
    'IS_INTERNSHIP',

    # Experience
    'MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE',
    'MAX_YEARS_EXPERIENCE',

    # Salary
    'SALARY_FROM',
    'SALARY_TO',

    # Geography (state dropped after red/blue join; city/MSA kept)
    'CITY_NAME',
    'MSA_NAME_INCOMING',

    # Industry — NAICS even levels only (2/4/6)
    'NAICS2',
    'NAICS2_NAME',
    'NAICS4',
    'NAICS4_NAME',
    'NAICS6',
    'NAICS6_NAME',

    # Skills
    'SKILLS',
    'SKILLS_NAME',
    'COMMON_SKILLS',
    'COMMON_SKILLS_NAME',
    'SOFTWARE_SKILLS',
    'SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME',

    # Occupation — legacy SOC broad + detailed (replaces SOC_2021_2 which is dropped)
    'SOC_2',
    'SOC_2_NAME',           # replaces SOC_2021_2_NAME
    'SOC_5',
    'SOC_5_NAME',
    'ONET',
    'ONET_NAME',

    # LOT taxonomy — career area level only
    'LOT_CAREER_AREA_NAME',
    'LOT_V6_CAREER_AREA',
    'LOT_V6_CAREER_AREA_NAME',
    'LOT_V6_OCCUPATION_GROUP',
    'LOT_V6_OCCUPATION_GROUP_NAME',

    # Lightcast sector
    'LIGHTCAST_SECTORS_NAME',

    # NAICS 2022 — even levels only (2/4/6)
    'NAICS_2022_2',
    'NAICS_2022_2_NAME',
    'NAICS_2022_4',
    'NAICS_2022_4_NAME',
    'NAICS_2022_6',
    'NAICS_2022_6_NAME',
]
    df_clean = df[keep_cols].copy()



    print("Shape after transform:", df_clean.shape)
    print("\nMissing values:\n", df_clean.isnull().sum())

    return df_clean

title: Machine Learning: Gender Wage Gap Decomposition
text:
Interpretation
Only 9.4% of the gender wage gap is explained by which occupation and industry someone works in. The remaining 90.6% persists even after accounting for job type, race, age and state. In other words, women in the same broad occupation and industry as men still earn substantially less. This isn’t simply because women are concentrated in lower-paying jobs. that’s a much stronger and more specific claim than ‘women earn less’ and it direclty supportsa story about unexplained disparity (potentially reflecting bias, negotiation gaps, promotion patterns, part-tme/full-time differences or other unmeasured factors)
The R² values are quite low (0.076 baseline, 0.259 full model), meaning the model only explains about 26% of the variation in wages overall — that’s normal for wage data (lots of individual variation), but it means the absolute dollar coefficients are more reliable as average effects across the whole population than as precise individual predictions. It’s fine to report the gender coefficient and decomposition percentage, but I’d avoid implying the model is highly accurate at predicting any one person’s wage.
The “unexplained” 90.6% almost certainly includes other unmeasured factors beyond pure discrimination — things like hours worked (full-time vs. part-time), years of experience, education level, and seniority within an occupation aren’t in your IPUMS table, so they get folded into the “unexplained” bucket too. It’s worth phrasing this carefully in your write-up, e.g. “after controlling for the variables available in this dataset” rather than claiming it’s pure bias.

text:
Antara: Gender Disparities in IT vs Overall Workforce (IPUMS & Lightcast)
This analysis focuses on comparing the IT workforce against the overall workforce using the 2024 IPUMS employment dataset and the Lightcast job postings dataset. The IT workforce is defined as workers with Census occupation codes between 1000 and 1999, which correspond to computer, mathematical, and information technology occupations — directly aligned with the types of roles captured in the Lightcast dataset.
The decision to compare IT workers specifically against the overall workforce — rather than other sectors such as healthcare, education, or finance — is intentional. The Lightcast dataset is heavily concentrated in IT and data-related job postings (over 93% of postings fall under Information Technology and Computer Science). By isolating IT workers in the IPUMS data and benchmarking them against the broader workforce, we can identify whether gender disparities in wages and representation are unique to the IT sector or reflect a wider systemic pattern. This cross-dataset perspective allows for a more meaningful and targeted analysis of gender hiring disparities in technology roles.

title: Predictive Modeling
text: This section presents our unsupervised model for the gender pay question: a K-Means clustering of the IPUMS workforce that groups workers into comparable labor-market segments by earnings and age. We then link those segments to employer demand from the Lightcast job postings through the one dimension the two datasets genuinely share, geography. The clustering complements the wage-gap regression in the companion analysis: the regression measures how large the gender gap is, while the clustering shows where in the wage distribution that gap concentrates.

title: Predictive Modeling
text: This section presents our unsupervised model for the gender pay question: a K-Means clustering of the IPUMS workforce that groups workers into comparable labor-market segments by earnings and age. We then link those segments to employer demand from the Lightcast job postings through the one dimension the two datasets genuinely share, geography. The clustering complements the wage-gap regression in the companion analysis: the regression measures how large the gender gap is, while the clustering shows where in the wage distribution that gap concentrates.

title: Predictive Modeling
text:
Methodology Note
The clustering and the state-level join are computed with Spark MLlib in analysis/ml_kmeans_julie.py and analysis/ml_state_join_julie.py, both built on the shared helpers in analysis/spark_utils.py. Running Spark on 1.57 million worker records is too heavy to execute on every site render, so the pipeline writes its results to data/processed/, and this page loads those saved outputs to present the figures. The features given to K-Means are annual wage income and age, both standardized because K-Means is distance based, and we select the number of clusters by silhouette score. All aggregates are weighted by the IPUMS person weight (PERWT) so the numbers reflect the population rather than the sample.


Code
import sys, pathlib
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.io as pio

# Consistent theme across every chart (project requirement).
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"

# Resolve the repo root from wherever Quarto executes, then reuse the
# shared plotly theme from analysis/utils.py (single styling source).
root = pathlib.Path.cwd()
while not (root / "_quarto.yml").exists() and root != root.parent:
    root = root.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(root / "analysis"))
from utils import apply_theme, PROCESSED

profile = pd.read_csv(PROCESSED / "kmeans_cluster_profile.csv")

# Label clusters by wage rank so names stay correct even if a re-run
# renumbers the clusters. This same mapping is reused everywhere below.
profile = profile.sort_values("wgt_avg_wage").reset_index(drop=True)
SEGMENTS = ["Low-wage, early career", "Mid-wage, late career",
            "High-wage professional", "Elite earners"]
profile["segment"] = SEGMENTS[: len(profile)]
profile["pct_female_disp"] = (profile["pct_female"] * 100).round(1)
cluster_to_segment = dict(zip(profile["cluster"], profile["segment"]))

How the clusters sit in the data
This scatter shows a random sample of workers placed by age and wage, the two features K-Means actually used, and colored by the segment they were assigned to. The large black diamonds mark each cluster’s centroid, which is the industry-standard term for the center point K-Means computes for a cluster. Reading it bottom to top, the algorithm separates workers into horizontal pay bands: a broad low-wage band, a mid-wage band, a high-wage professional band, and a sparse elite band far above the rest. This is the visual meaning of the clusters, namely neighborhoods of workers who earn and age similarly. A full-data version of this graph that plots all 1.57 million workers is available in the runnable notebook analysis/ml_kmeans_julie.ipynb; the website uses a representative sample so the page stays light.


Code
samp = pd.read_csv(PROCESSED / "kmeans_scatter_sample.csv")
samp["segment"] = samp["cluster"].map(cluster_to_segment)

fig = px.scatter(
    samp, x="AGE", y="INCWAGE", color="segment",
    category_orders={"segment": SEGMENTS}, opacity=0.45,
    labels={"AGE": "Age", "INCWAGE": "Annual wage (USD)", "segment": "Segment"},
    title="K-Means segments in the age-by-wage space",
)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=profile["wgt_avg_age"], y=profile["wgt_avg_wage"],
    mode="markers", marker=dict(symbol="diamond", size=14, color="black"),
    name="Centroid", hovertext=profile["segment"], hoverinfo="text",
))
apply_theme(fig)
fig.show()


                            
                                            
Worker sample in the age-by-wage feature space, colored by K-Means segment. Black diamonds are cluster centroids. The clusters form distinct horizontal pay bands.


The clearest pattern is that the female share falls as segment pay rises. Women make up close to half of the low-wage and mid-wage segments, around a third of the high-wage professional segment, and under a quarter of the elite-earning segment. The chart below shows the female and male shares side by side within each segment. Because the IPUMS sex variable records only male or female, the male share is the exact complement of the female share, so the two series mirror each other and carry the same information. We show both because the crossover is the point: as pay rises the female bars shrink and the male bars grow, so the two genders trade places between the bottom and the top of the wage distribution. This is the structural backdrop the wage-gap regression then quantifies.


Code
gp = profile[["segment", "pct_female_disp"]].copy()
gp["Female"] = gp["pct_female_disp"]
gp["Male"] = (100 - gp["pct_female_disp"]).round(1)
gender_long = gp.melt(id_vars="segment", value_vars=["Female", "Male"],
                      var_name="Sex", value_name="pct")
fig = px.bar(
    gender_long, x="segment", y="pct", color="Sex", barmode="group",
    category_orders={"segment": SEGMENTS, "Sex": ["Female", "Male"]},
    color_discrete_map={"Female": "#d7191c", "Male": "#2c7bb6"},
    labels={"segment": "", "pct": "% of segment", "Sex": ""},
    title="Female vs male share by wage segment",
)
fig.add_hline(y=50, line_dash="dash", line_color="#666",
              annotation_text="50% (parity)")
apply_theme(fig)
fig.show()


                            
                                            
Weighted female and male share within each wage segment, with a 50 percent parity reference line. Female representation falls and male representation rises as segment pay increases; the two are complements because sex is recorded as binary.

title: Predictive Modeling
section: Step 2: Linking Segments to Employer Demand
text:
Step 2: Linking Segments to Employer Demand
Step 2 takes the worker segments from Step 1 and asks a geographic question. For every state we attach two kinds of information, the supply side from IPUMS, meaning how its workers are spread across the four segments and how female each segment is, and the demand side from Lightcast, meaning how many job postings that state generated. The single shared key is the state, so the join happens at the state level. The views below move from an interactive map that lets you explore any segment and either sex, to a direct political comparison.


Code
sc = pd.read_csv(PROCESSED / "state_cluster_demand.csv")
sc["segment"] = sc["cluster"].map(cluster_to_segment)
sc["pct_female_disp"] = (sc["pct_female"] * 100).round(1)
top_segment = profile.iloc[-1]["segment"]          # highest-wage segment
top_cluster = profile.iloc[-1]["cluster"]



The interactive map: female or male share by segment and state
The map below is the supply side made explorable. Use the dropdown to choose any of the four segments together with either the female or the male share, and the choropleth recolors to that selection. Red versus blue states
Because the gender pathway asks about political influence, we also split states by their 2024 presidential result and compare the female share of the top-pay segment in blue states against red states. So that the comparison is self-explanatory, the first map below colors each state by which party carried it in 2024, giving the political geography directly rather than asking the reader to recall it. The second chart then compares the female share of the top-pay segment across those two groups. Here a modest difference does appear: blue states average close to twenty-five percent female in the top-pay segment while red states sit closer to twenty-two percent. The direction fits expectations, with women somewhat better represented at the top in blue-leaning states, but the gap between the two is small and both groups remain far below parity. So politics nudges the result a little, whereas employer demand did not, and neither comes close to closing the structural shortfall the map reveals nationwide.

title: Predictive Modeling
text:
Implications for Job Seekers
For a woman targeting the highest-paying segment of the labor market, these results suggest that the odds of reaching that segment move very little with how active a state’s hiring market is, and only modestly with its political leaning, where blue-leaning states show a small edge. Across every view the imbalance holds well below parity, so none of these levers comes close to closing it. The more useful levers are the ones the companion regression points to, namely the occupation and industry a person enters and the unexplained gap that persists even within the same kind of work. The clustering reframes the question from how much women earn on average to which earning tiers they are able to reach, and every view here shows the barrier sitting at the top of the wage distribution.

title: Predictive Modeling
text:
Caveats
The Lightcast salary is an advertised figure that signals demand, while the IPUMS wage is what workers actually earned, so the two are reported separately and never averaged together. Employer demand is measured at the state level because the two datasets do not share occupation coding, which means a state’s posting volume repeats across that state’s worker segments by design and supports a state-level comparison rather than a person-level one. The red and blue grouping reflects the 2024 presidential result and is a coarse proxy for political climate. The analysis is a single cross-sectional snapshot of roughly 2023 to 2024 rather than a trend.
